notes.claim: A schematic gives the functional information of a system and does not accurately show where its components are.
Each symbol on a fluid power diagram is drawn to show the normal or neutral condition of its component, unless several diagrams show other phases.
A circuit diagram does not show what a circuit actually looks like, or how long its connections are.
Lines that simply cross do not show an electrical connection unless they are marked with a small circle.
A schematic supplies the functional information of a system, not the relative location of its components.
An open failure in the wiring or a solenoid coil is the likeliest fault, so a system should be designed to be in its safest mode with the solenoid de-energised.
An electrical one-line diagram outlines connections from power sources through a distribution system to the loads that use the power.
A one-line diagram typically starts at the top with the incoming power and its disconnecting device, and works down.
On a one-line diagram, one line shown for a bus or cable represents all three phases.
A coil and its contacts may appear on different pages or rungs, so they are matched by reference designation and cross-reference information.
A normally closed contact is drawn closed even when, in normal running, its coil is energised and the contact is open.
Permissive contacts are wired in series, so that if any one of them detects an unsafe condition, the circuit is opened.
Hydraulic graphical symbols give no information about how a component is built.
A pump and a motor symbol differ only in where the arrow touches the circle: the point for a pump, the tail for a motor.
Fluid power symbols may be rotated or reversed without changing their meaning, except for lines to reservoirs and vented manifolds.
A 4-way valve has four pipe connections, generally pressure, return, port A and port B; a two-position valve can sit in either of two switched positions.
A valve is drawn in its de-actuated state, and the diagram can also show it operated, with the flow it then gives.
With a 5/2 valve operated, supply pressure goes to the piston side of the cylinder while the piston-rod side is exhausted, and the rod advances.
A double-acting hydraulic cylinder takes fluid in either chamber, and while one chamber is pressurised the other is lined up to drain back to the reservoir.
Piping and instrument drawings show valves in their normal position unless stated otherwise, usually the primary flowpath of the system.
A checklist for safe isolation asks whether the isolation points on the plant match the line diagram and isolation certificate.
Gate and globe valves are often drawn with the same symbol; the valve's tag number or the drawing's notes and legend may say which it is.
A diaphragm actuator's symbol alone does not say whether air pressure opens or closes the valve.
A three-way valve is sometimes drawn in the position it fails to, not its normal position.
When a print shows two piping systems of the same kind, extra letters on the symbols tell them apart.
Engineering components are three-dimensional but drawings and screens are two-dimensional, which is why a part is shown as several views.
Either first or third angle projection can be chosen, but a technician should understand the principles of both.
The first step in reading a fluid power diagram is to get an overall view of what is happening.
A schematic shows function rather than location, and each symbol shows a normal or neutral condition, so a new diagram is read for function and drawn state.
A one-line diagram is read from the incoming supply down to the loads.
